Adult females of the Montseny brook newt (Calotriton arnoldi) attain a maximum snout-vent length of 6.8 centimeters [Li = 6.8 centimeters], a measurement that represents the ultimate body size for this species and is consistent with the relatively small body plan characteristic of stream-dwelling salamandrids. Sexual maturation occurs considerably earlier, with individuals reaching puberty at a snout-vent length of 5.2 centimeters [Lp = 5.2 centimeters], reflecting a substantial growth phase between the onset of reproductive capacity and the achievement of final adult dimensions. This size differential between pubertal and ultimate stages suggests that post-maturational growth contributes significantly to the overall body size of older females.

Newly hatched larvae emerge from their gelatinous egg capsules at a remarkably modest body mass, with wet weight at birth measuring just 0.0654 grams [Wwb = 0.0654 grams]. This low initial mass is typical of urodele species that produce relatively small, nutrient-rich eggs, and it imposes a substantial challenge for the endotrophic larva during its early development. The yolk-dependent tadpole must absorb its endogenous reserves efficiently before the onset of exogenous feeding, a critical transition that will determine its subsequent growth trajectory. Comparative data from congeneric species indicate that this birth weight is within the expected range for a newt of this adult body size.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], females produce approximately one clutch per year. Each clutch contains roughly 30 eggs [N_R_i = Each clutch contains roughly 30 eggs], and the annual reproductive frequency is approximately one clutch per year [F_R_i = approximately one clutch per year]. This relatively low annual fecundity is consistent with the life-history strategy of a long-lived, slow-maturing amphibian that invests in a small number of offspring per breeding season. The reproductive rate at this thermal regime probably reflects an energetic ceiling imposed by the cold, oligotrophic mountain streams the species inhabits, where prey availability is seasonally limited and metabolic costs are elevated.

Adults display a pronounced size dimorphism, with gravid females reaching an ultimate wet weight of 3 grams [Wwi = 3 grams], a mass that represents the maximum recorded body weight for the species and is attained only after several years of post-pubertal growth. In contrast, the wet weight at puberty is approximately 1.48 grams [Wwp = approximately 1.48 grams], indicating that individuals have more than doubled their body mass between the onset of sexual maturation and the achievement of asymptotic size. This substantial mass increase reflects the progressive accumulation of somatic tissues and energy reserves necessary to support the high energetic demands of reproduction and overwintering in the cold headwater streams of the Montseny massif. At a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the time since birth at puberty is estimated at about 3 years since birth [tp = about 3 years since birth], a developmental period that represents a significant fraction of the total lifespan and underscores the slow pace of life history in this cold-adapted species.

Longevity records for Calotriton arnoldi indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 11 years [am = approximately 11 years] under natural conditions, though captive individuals of the closely related Calotriton asper have been documented living for at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]up to 26 years. The extended juvenile phase observed in this newt may be an adaptive response to the low productivity and thermal constraints of the species' montane habitat, allowing individuals to accumulate sufficient body mass and energy stores before committing to reproductive effort. This life-history strategy, characterized by a late onset of reproduction and a prolonged reproductive lifespan, is commonly observed in urodeles inhabiting cold, stable environments where annual reproductive output is limited but individual survival is high.
